subject: giraffe
pitch: A young reticulated giraffe. Chestnut patches outlined by bright cream lines all over its body and neck, a short mane of stiff brown hair down the neck, two fuzzy ossicones with black tufts on top, big ears, long lashes, a long dark tongue just peeking out, and slender legs fading to cream above the hooves.
reasoning:
I need to build a single TypeScript module using the SDK, sticking closely to the documented API surface like joints, chains, sweeps, lofts, and parts rather than guessing at unlisted features, while keeping the file reasonably compact but solid.

I'm weighing which primitives are safe to rely on versus riskier ones with uncertain signatures, settling on joint, chain, sweep, part, stick, spike, surface, ring, along, rng, frame, and line as the dependable set. For surface patches like markings, I'm planning to use surface.nearest to find attachment points and stick flattened geometry onto the body along the normal, possibly approximating outlines with small sequences of boxes along a closed path rather than relying on unverified texture or paint functions.

Now I'm sketching proportions for the giraffe model — overall height, body barrel position and length, neck and head placement, and leg span from body to hooves — then working out the joint hierarchy, starting with a root body joint and child chains for the spine and neck, while reasoning through how chain and sweep might interact via path frames to build the tubular limb and neck geometry.

Since the chain and sweep APIs feel uncertain, I decide to fall back on safer, directly-controlled geometry: using scaled sphere shapes for body parts rather than relying on loft or chain-based tube generation, since I can manually scale and position basic primitives with more confidence in how the part system attaches them to bones.

For the skeleton, I'm setting up joints with explicit parent references, building a hip root and branching into chest/neck joints and then leg joints per side, since the parent option is the safest documented way to build hierarchy. For limbs, I decide against the uncertain limb-helper or rod/capsule functions and instead plan to connect joint points with simple geometric parts.

Legs will use sweep paths through hip-knee-ankle points with a single radius, accepting the simplification that they'll be fairly rigid and not tapered. I'm settling on a warm fawn/tan base coat with chestnut patches, cream outline accents, dark mane and ossicone tufts, and near-black hooves and eyes for a young giraffe's coloring, planning to place the patches onto the body surface using nearest-point lookups.

For the cream outlines around each patch, I'm working out how to avoid z-fighting by offsetting the patch slightly along the surface normal above the cream disc beneath it, though I'm uncertain exactly how the geometry gets seated and oriented on the surface — I'll just assume a Y-up convention with the base at the origin and proceed from there.

Now I need a surface to project onto for the body itself, since surface() requires some source geometry. I'm considering building the torso as a sweep along a path with a given radius, treating that tube as the body surface even though caps and tapering are uncertain, and just accepting the approximation rather than figuring out loft station formats.

For the neck I'm leaning toward another sweep with a slightly bigger radius to look thick, with the head as a separate part. For the mane, I'm thinking of placing a row of small spike shapes along the back of the neck sweep, finding hit points via nearest-point queries and orienting each spike's direction roughly upward and backward along the crest, even though I don't have exact normal data to work from.

For ossicones I'm planning two small cylinder/cone bumps on top of the head with tiny black sphere tufts at their tips. For ears I'm picturing flattened cone shapes rotated and placed on the sides of the head. For eyes I'm considering a black sphere with a manual ring of tiny rotated boxes around it to fake lashes, since I'm unsure of a built-in ring helper's exact signature.

I'm using the dir option in the part function to orient geometry along a direction, which helps for aiming the lashes upward and outward. The tongue becomes a thin sweep from the mouth outward.

For the legs, I'm sketching slender limb sweeps: an upper tan segment from hip to knee, a lower cream segment from knee to ankle, and a small dark hoof box at the bottom, with front legs offset forward and back legs offset backward along the z-axis, positioned at roughly ±0.28 in x to sit under the body.

I'm reworking the overall body proportions to look more giraffe-like — raising the body center for longer legs, tilting the neck forward from chest to head, and placing ossicones near the top of the skull. I'm now setting up a joint hierarchy: a body root joint, then a neck base, neck top, and head joint chained together, so the neck sweep can bend naturally along that chain.

For patch placement on the body surface, I'm generating approximate points and letting a nearest-surface projection snap them onto the actual mesh, rather than computing exact surface coordinates myself.

I'm distributing patches around the body, using angle and height variation while skipping the belly region, and similarly placing a smaller cluster of patches along the neck's centerline with slight offsets so they sit naturally on the surface.

For the mane, I'm spacing spike geometry along the neck crest to create stiff, short brown hair, and for the ears, I'm placing flattened, angled spheres at the sides of the head so they point outward and slightly back like real animal ears.

Now I'm shaping the head itself as an elongated sphere with a tan muzzle box, a cream-colored lighter tone for giraffe-style features, and a dark tongue sweeping out from the mouth, then positioning small black eye spheres and lash details on the sides of the head while making sure they don't clash with the nearby ear placement.

Next I'm adding ossicones as small sweeps rising from the top of the head in a fawn/brown tone, topped with fuzzy black tuft spheres, plus dark cylindrical hooves at the base of each leg attached simply to the body bone for simplicity. I'm also considering whether to add a short tail with a tuft for completeness even though it wasn't explicitly requested.

Then I'm structuring the legs as layered sweeps -- a thin tan upper segment, a blended mid-tone transition, and a cream lower segment -- to create a natural color fade down each slender leg, while deciding against extra knee joints to keep things simple.

I'm finalizing the color palette (fawn base, dark brown patches, cream underbelly, near-black mane and tuft, muted ossicone tone) and shaping the body sweep from chest to rear, adding a rounded sphere at the rump for a fuller silhouette.

Now I'm setting up the build function itself -- importing the builder utilities, seeding the random generator, and defining the named color constants before starting to assemble the giraffe's geometry piece by piece.

Setting up body joints and sweep shapes...

Adding ossicones with horn sweeps and tufts, a tongue sweep curving down from the mouth, and now building the legs as layered sweeps from fawn to cream shading, ending in hoof cylinders.

For patches I'm using scaled sphere geometries to create flat circular markings with raised rims, then setting up an array of body points distributed around the torso by z-position and angle to place them.

Adding patches for the neck and sides, with random skipping to avoid a too-regular pattern, keeping total part count well under budget. For surface placement I'm computing nearest points against the body tube surface source to position each patch accurately.

Placing side and top patches along the neck...

I'm figuring out how to render the mane spikes along the neck crest, projecting points onto the neck surface and angling them up and back, but I'm unsure about the exact spike function signature and whether it accepts a color argument -- leaning toward using a stick with a cone geometry instead for more control over color.

I'll use similarly offset cone or sphere geometries for other features like patches and ossicones, skipping extra details like eye rings for now, and finish by returning the root with the required metadata export.

Now I'm drafting the actual TypeScript module: setting up imports, defining color constants, and building the skeleton joints for body, neck, and head, followed by the torso path geometry.

Still writing geometry setup...

Writing patch helper function...

Still computing patch positions...

There's slight overlap near the neck base where the patch angles meet the body, but that's minor. For the legs, I'm looping over left/right sides and front/back z-positions to place each leg symmetrically.

For ears, I'm working out the rotation math so each ear tilts outward and backward correctly — checking the sign conventions so the +X ear and -X ear both end up with tips pointing backward rather than crossing in the wrong direction.

I'm now placing the ossicones with their horn-colored sweep paths and fur tufts, attaching them to the head bone, then double-checking leg geometry so the hooves taper properly from top to bottom and sit flush with the ground.

For the tongue, I'm sweeping a thin dark path emerging from the muzzle box so it peeks out naturally without clipping through the mouth geometry. Then I'm working out eyelash placement using small flat boxes arranged in a slight curve along the eye socket, followed by the eye ellipsoids sized to sit partially embedded in the head sphere for a believable eye socket look.

I'm skipping any cream stripe detail on the muzzle to keep things simple, and now I'm finalizing the full assembly, making sure the root node is returned and double-checking there's no stray unused import like lerp before writing out the complete code.
